chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, and Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, from Hammad ibn 'Uthman, from Is'haq ibn 'Ammar who said:

I asked Abu Ibrahim (peace be upon him) about the man who takes a security deposit for a mortgage of one hundred Dirhams and it is equated to three hundred Dirhams, so it is destroyed. Is it upon the man that he returns to his companion two hundred Dirhams? He (peace be upon him) said: 'Yes, because he took a deposit wherein was excess, and wasted it.' I said, 'Supposing half the deposit was destroyed?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'It would be upon the reckoning of that.' I said, 'So they would both be returning the excess?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'Yes'.
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling if a pledged item is destroyed while in the creditor's possession?
ai.summary: This narration from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies the principle of *ghurm bi al-ghurm* (liability corresponds to benefit) in Islamic finance, establishing that the creditor bears the risk of loss for the collateral's value exceeding the debt. It highlights the Shia juristic emphasis on fairness, ensuring the creditor does not unjustly retain the 'excess' value (*fadl*) of the pledged item if it perishes while in their custody. This ruling serves as a foundational precedent for modern Islamic banking contracts involving collateral and risk allocation.
